Mocking ESM Modules

This project's native-ESM Jest setup can't use the familiar jest.mock() — unstable_mockModule plus a dynamic import stand in for it.

Having a fake mockPrisma object (previous slide) only helps if ticket.service.js actually receives it instead of the real src/config/db.js singleton. In most Jest tutorials, that's jest.mock(), called with a static import at the top of the file — but that technique relies on Babel rewriting your code first, and this project's Jest setup deliberately runs Node's real ES modules directly instead (--experimental- vm-modules, the test script from Lesson 1's Jest topic) — no Babel step exists to make jest.mock()'s usual trick work.

The native-ESM equivalent is jest.unstable_mockModule(), paired with a dynamic import() instead of a static one:

// Figure 2.19: swapping db.js for a fake (tests/unit/ticket.service.test.js, excerpt)
jest.unstable_mockModule('../../src/config/db.js', () => ({
  default: mockPrisma,
}));

const { getAllTickets, getTicketById, createTicket } = await import(
  '../../src/services/ticket.service.js'
);

Order matters here in a way it doesn't with ordinary imports: import statements at the top of a file are hoisted and resolved before anything else runs, so a static import of ticket.service.js would already have pulled in the real db.js before jest.mock() ever got a chance to intervene. Calling jest.unstable_mockModule() first, then using await import(...) — a plain expression, not hoisted — guarantees the mock is registered before ticket.service.js is loaded at all, so when it does its own import prisma from '../config/db.js' (Figure 2.14), it receives mockPrisma instead of ever constructing a real PrismaClient.

The default: mockPrisma shape matters too: db.js uses export default prisma (the client-as-a-singleton topic), so the fake module needs the same default export to stand in for it convincingly.
